b: Pure originality was a modernist dream. Ordinary language is notoriously built out of clichés—words and expressions that have been used so often we hardly see them anymore. They grow like dandelions, unnoticed until suddenly they’re all over the place. Somewhere John Updike called for a moratorium on the word “stunning,” a word he then continued to use. A famous essay in The New Yorker pointed out that the magazine’s editors seemed to favor poems about water. Trying to write a piece of fiction without clichés is like Dorothy of Oz setting out to cross the poppy field: she won’t make it, sooner or later she’ll fall asleep. A few writers can soldier on like the Straw Man and the Tin Man, writing page after page without noticeable clichés. Ali Smith, Anne Carson, Will Self, and Nicholson Baker can do that. Paul Celan may hold the title of Most Immune to Clichés: he literally disassembled words in order to avoid conventional words in the German language, which he felt was indelibly soiled.

Winnowing prose from its cliché infestation is an endless task. It’s just as difficult to avoid stereotypical plotlines. Traumatized child finds difficult redemption, tragedy first rends then restores a couple’s relationship, journey transforms an uncertain girl into a strong-willed adult. Readers expect to recognize the sort of plot a novel uses, and to enjoy the author’s variations. Stereotypical plotlines are more pervasive even than clichés, because not many writers even think of evading them, and the ones who do frequently fail. It’s hard to think up a genuinely new narrative. Nabokov was especially good at it. When he wrote Lolita, there was nothing like it, and when he died he was at work on The Original of Laura, another original plot. He loved dismaying his readers. He once said he wished someone would write a novel about a serial killer who lives happily into old age, with an adoring family and happy grandchildren.

Genre is the third kind of cliché. There are websites that list dozens: the YA, the Scandi noir, chick lit, mystery, thriller, horror, Westerns, historical fiction, alternative history, hard and soft science fiction, litRPG, steampunk, space opera, crime fiction, police procedural, courtroom drama. One of the peculiarities of publishing is that the category “literary fiction” lumps all of those under the heading of “genre,” as if a literary novel doesn’t fit any mold. But few authors of “literary fiction” have managed to write novels that avoid genres.

These three sources of unoriginality—clichés, plotlines, and genres—are my rough guides. When a book successfully avoids them, it can appear genuinely original. It’s not something every reader or writer wants: after all, there is enormous appeal in familiar plotlines, provided they’re cleverly tweaked. It isn’t always interesting or advisable to avoid genre (think of Stephen King, or Agatha Christie), and virtually everyone speaks, at least sometimes, in clichés. But originality can be incredibly seductive.

These are the books I often pull down from my shelves while I write. They show me ways to evade any number of formulas, clichés, commonplaces, and stereotypes. If you’d like to experience what reading is like when the book is really outside the box, here are some of the least conventional novels of the last hundred years.

One consequence of having read Watt after all of Beckett’s other novels is that now I’m bewildered that he is so widely appreciated. I can understand the popularity of Godot, and I can see his postwar works as examples of existentialism, but I am baffled that a book as bizarre, as emotionally and affectively opaque, as formally unaccountable, as multiply wrecked and fragmented, as little in control of its logic as Watt could ever come to be widely understood as a classic of the kind that attracts Nobel committees. Watt makes Flann O’Brien’s nearly dissociative fantasies like The Third Policeman (coming up below) seem homey and congenial. Watt makes Daniel Paul Schreber’s Memoirs of My Nervous Illness, written while its author was institutionalized for psychosis, seem like a sentimental diary.

This is a novel of barely managed compulsions, of nearly uncontrolled and effectively meaningless experiences. The narrator is like a helium balloon tethered to his own life by an unraveling thread. He secures and re-secures his experiences to their meanings by rehearsing self-imposed conditions and games. He finds it especially comforting to run through lists. Entire pages of Watt are manic formulas separated by commas:

Not that Watt felt calm and free and glad, for he did not.. but he thought that perhaps he felt calm and free and glad, or if not calm and free and glad, at least calm and free, or free and glad, or glad and calm, or if not calm and free, or free and glad, or glad and calm, or if not calm and free, or free and glad, or glad and calm…

I doubt Beckett could have produced anything resembling an explanation for the structure of his book. The scholar Hayman says it is “astonishing” to discover Beckett had “no idea where he was going, no project, no outline, no plot, no setting, and effectively no characters: tabula rasa.” This is really as close to idiocy as literary criticism gets. Of course it is not astonishing to learn Beckett did not know where he was going with Watt. By the fifth page any reader who is listening for something other than a clue or a key or a plot knows this is desperate stuff. Watt is so far beyond conventions, so far outside of clichés, that you see early on that it won’t be a matter of understanding the book, only coping with it.
César Aira, How I Became a Nun (and all his other books)

The first two chapters of this short book are absolutely excruciating to read. Incredibly well managed and funny, but also weird and tense. The narrator is a boy, but then again, he might be a girl. That’s strange enough, because the ambiguity is managed offhandedly; someone refers to the protagonist as “he,” and someone else as “she.” The child is offered a strawberry ice cream. It’s a special treat, because he, or she, has never had ice cream. The child nearly gags on it, and Aira’s description is intense and nauseating. The father doubts his child, argues, and gets angry. Every child in the world likes strawberry ice cream! he says. He forces his child to have another spoonful.

I felt the ice cream dissolving, and my whole body was seized by a convulsion… disgust flooded through me… another big spoonful was on the way, I opened my mouth. I was already crying, Dad put the spoon in my free hand.
I choked, coughed, and began to wail…
“Don’t like it? Eh? din’t you like it? You’re a moron, you know that?”
Finally the father tastes the ice cream himself—and realizes it’s poison. He flies into a rage and kills the ice-cream vendor.

There’s nothing like those first two chapters. After that, the book goes the way many of Aira’s books go: in the unpredictable directions of his meandering imagination. Aira writes short novels, lots and lots of them, and he’s said he never plans and never revises. The books vary in their magic. Is it against the rules of the list if I propose that a series of his little books can count as a single kaleidoscopic novel? I would pick four more to go with this one. They can all be read in an evening.

An Episode in the Life of a Landscape Painter is taken from a real-life memoir, but you’d never know it because of the arresting way he tells the story of a man struck by lightning and dragged by his horse until he is deformed. Ghosts is a spectacularly strange story of naked, paunchy, middle-aged male ghosts who just hang around without frightening anyone. Sometimes they pose as the hands of clocks, and other times people snag their penises by mistake. The Literary Conference is about a man who solves an ancient mystery and finds a treasure chest, which he then completely forgets and goes on with his life.

The best of Aira’s books are like an encyclopedia of ways to evade clichés. The rest of the time he’s meandering, and he staves off stereotypes just by shutting down one plotline and taking up another.
Walter Abish, Alphabetical Africa, and Raymond Roussel, Impressions of Africa
These are two books that are supposedly about Africa, but are actually more about their authors’ weird senses of what novels might be.

The chapters in Abish’s book go from A to Z and back to A, and each one uses only a subset of letters of the alphabet. The first chapter has only words beginning with a; the second has words beginning with a and b, and so forth. The book begins:
Ages ago, Alex, Allen and Alva arrived at Antibes, and Alva allowing all, allowing anyone, against Alex’s admonition, against Allen’s angry assertion: another African amusement…
When he gets to z, Abish goes backwards to a, and then the book ends. By the time he ends he seems pretty tired:
Another abbreviation another abdomen another abduction another aberration another abhorrent ass another abnormal act…

And yet this last chapter (which goes on for two pages) also reads like a summary of the book. In the middle he has more latitude for stories. Abish said he wrote the book to express his “distrust of the understanding that is intrinsic in any communication,” and the characters sometimes ponder that. Here is the opening of the first chapter titled “M,” with words that begin with m or with any letter in the alphabet before m:
My memory isn’t accurate anymore. Mentioning my memory makes me feel insecure. A few months ago Alex and Allen kidnapped a jeweler in Antibes and killed him almost inadvertently…
Making memory more meaningful in darkest Africa, a certain Chief Auwick measures all meaning in his former life.

By the letter g or h you know you won’t learn anything about Africa, or even anything worthwhile as fiction, and you know the author is really interested in how communication doesn’t work the way people think. You watch how he navigates his rules about the first letters of words, and at the same time you read his stories, and you never really understand how the two things are related. The experience of reading remains odd start to finish. What game is this author playing, exactly?

All the Africa references in Alphabetical Africa are fake, of course, and in that Abish is following Raymond Roussel’s Impressions of Africa, an even crazier book, which also has nothing to do with Africa. Lots has been written about Roussel, so I’ll just say that the book is supposedly about some European who are shipwrecked in Africa. While they wait to be rescued, they put on an entertainment for the king who is hosting them. But it’s not really about that. The first half of the book is a series of disconnected descriptions of intricate bizarre sculptures, dances, and performances. A statue of Emmanuel Kant made of cuttlefish bones, standing on railroad tracks made of veal lungs. A coral bracelet, which is actually a huge worm, trained by a Hungarian man to play the zither. A man who sings Frère Jacques in four voices from the corners of his mouth. For the entire first half of the book you read minute descriptions of these things, one after the other. The second half explains how the sculpture was constructed, how the worm was trained, and so on, but in the end everything’s as weird and unmotivated as it was at the beginning. No one finishes reading Roussel and says, Oh, okay, now it makes perfect sense. Roussel is an entire world—his next book, New Impressions of Africa, which is also not about Africa, took him seventeen years—and he needs to be read to be believed.

Christine Brooke-Rose was one of twentieth century England’s finest eccentrics. Reading her is like being in a seminar room and you’re the only student. She talks continuously, and you scramble to keep up. Thru is full of names and ideas. It was published in 1975, when Brooke-Rose was working in Paris and absorbing French literary theory, philosophy, and linguistics. The book ends with a five-page long list of what appears to be every proper name in the book. Here’s part of it. (I’ve annotated a few of her entries.)
Quipu [ancient Andean accounting method using knotted string]
Rastignac [character in Balzac’s La Comédie humaine]
Ruwet, Nicholas [a Belgian linguist and critic who died in 2001]
At the end she grades everyone from A+ to F (except that she uses Greek letters). It’s the teacher’s verdict, as if she’s making her own canon of literature.

Thru takes place around a literary conference, and it’s about what kinds of books people should write. At one point the narrator gives us a sort of moral: “The two pleasures, the pleasure in your game and the curiosity, should be skillfully balanced which is the work of a lifetime.” The book is full of curiosities and games. Many pages look more like diagrams than typed prose. There are concrete (shaped) poems, acrostics (where certain letters in words combine to form hidden sentences), mesostics (where you read down from line to line to discover hidden sentences), and pages that look like the Olympic rings, with letters in linked circles.

When I read Brooke-Rose, I always think how isolated she must have been, how determined. When she wrote this there were very few precedents for pages with experimental layouts. She was a scholar of Ezra Pound, and his Cantos do a little of what she did. There was also Guillaume Apollinaire, who pioneered concrete poetry, and the now mostly forgotten Maurice Roche, who used graphics and found text in his book Compact (1966). But really she was by herself, out at the end of the limb, writing for very few people.

If modernism wasn’t so serious—if Woolf, Joyce, and the others weren’t so sure of their importance—then this book would be more often read alongside Stein’s Making of Americans or Joyce’s Finnegans Wake as a prewar work that is so radical that it seems postmodern. But Gombrowicz is insecure, mortified, obsessive, skittish, and ticklish. The closest to Ferdydurke in this respect may be Flann O’Brien’s At Swim-Two-Birds, published two years after Ferdydurke in 1939. Both novels are vertiginously out of control, and full of hysterical humor.

Ferdydurke’s protagonist is a serious young novelist who cares about form, and there is a long interpolated chapter in the author’s voice, theorizing the importance of structure to ambitious literature. Yet the book is dedicated to a theme that makes all that seem very far away: Gombrowicz is interested in the fragile, undependable feeling that a young boy or girl has when they’ve just realized they might be grown up. At any moment their grown-up façade might shatter, and everyone will see the frantic, ridiculous, misshapen world they inhabit, with is bottomless embarrassments, awkwardnesses, itches, giggles, blushes, and toilet noises. In Gombrowicz’s language, if a group of children pesters you until you pee your pants or otherwise embarrass yourself, you’ve been “dealt the pupa”—revealed as a grub.

By comparison with Gombrowicz, major modernist authors come across as stolid and determinedly mature. By comparison with the acidic comedy in this book, most attempts at comic fiction, from John Barth or Thomas Pynchon to Adam Levin or Charlie Kaufman, sound like professional scripted stand-up.
Michael Cawood Green, Sinking: A Verse Novella

This is a mixture of poetry, song lyrics, historical narrative, essays and a glossary, supposedly written by various people. It concerns an actual event, a sinkhole that appeared in a mining community called Blyvooruitzicht in South Africa in 1964 and swallowed a house, killing five people. At first it seems the book might be a versified report. It opens with twenty-one poems, most about people who died or were involved in the event. One is about a washing machine shown in a photo “poised inches from the edge of the half-house / Not taken by the ‘sinkholegrave’.”

The second half of the book opens with six short poems on the ethics of writing poetry about tragedies. (“If I could turn all this / Into poetry / Would they forgive me? / — for getting it all wrong”). Then there’s commentary supposedly written by several other people, and finally a prose essay called “The Secret History of Sinking,” signed by Michael Green. The book concludes with a “supplement” of Green’s song lyrics.

It’s the mixture that makes this so memorable. Instead of the facts about people and houses, we get poems, and instead of a nonfiction explanation we get the author’s doubts and songs. On the back cover is an aerial photograph of the pit into which the houses fell.

There are echoes of many older writers. I thought of William Carlos Williams’s Paterson, his book-length verse and prose account of Paterson, New Jersey. Walter Benjamin’s attempts to capture nineteenth-century Paris in newspaper clippings is also in the air, and so are modernist poets like Wallace Stevens. I don’t think Green knew two of the closest parallels: Paul Metcalf (my next entry), and Hans Magnus Enzensberger’s wonderful book-length poem The Sinking of the Titanic.

But in the end, as with any strong book, none of that matters. Sinking isn’t famous, but its mixture of memoir, self-doubt, faked documentation, and Afrikaans is not easily forgotten, and in a period that’s flooded with talk about the fiction-nonfiction boundary, that is a rare accomplishment.
Paul Metcalf, U.S. Department of the Interior

Metcalf was an expert on his famous great-grandfather Herman Melville. Metcalf wrote in Melville’s house, at Melville’s desk, and thought a lot about how to write experimental American fiction in the twentieth century. The book opens with a chapter about an earthquake in Alaska. Then we’re plunged into an apparently entirely disconnected chapter on the symptoms of migraine. Three pages into it we’re given a list of symptoms:
an edging of light of a zigzag shape and curruscating [sic: coruscating] at right angles to its length
stars, circles, squares or squiggles, throbbing, spinning, flickering and spinning
in a visual storm, a brilliant sand dune, the brains shimmering
The next line suddenly connects migraines to the earthquake:
a road cracking up with a severe earthquake

This is a surprising and beautifully managed return to his opening descriptions of Alaskan roads breaking up in the earthquake. The earthquake is relived, in the reader’s eye, as a scotoma, an abstract vision. When I first read this I turned back to the beginning and started again. In retrospect, the transition is set up by the last section of the preceding earthquake chapter, which is about how Houston was lifted four inches by a surface wave from the Alaska quake, 3,300 miles away: a signal to the reader that distant connections will reappear.

Metcalf should be required reading for all MFA students, because he takes even the most attentive reader to school, demonstrating how to make connections that aren’t forced, programmatic, obvious, or awkward. It’s no wonder that in interviews and essays, Metcalf said Melville wrote poetry in prose, even if his actual poetry was awful, and that people like Melville and Poe knew they were blurring the boundaries of poetry and prose. Both those forms, poetry and prose, and blended and changed in Metcalf’s work.

At first read this book seems to be patently crazy, meaning both hallucinatory and dissociative. Almost every page has oddities like knives so thin they can’t be seen, microscopic carved wooden boxes, and bicycles that have sexes and change from one to another. There’s a smell machine that “splits up any smell into its sub- and inter-smells,” revealing “the dirty smells that are inside” perfume.
Everyone has a theory about the book. There are at least five principal explanations:
(1) O’Brien is the forgotten Irish modernist, the one who didn’t leave Ireland. The Third Policeman is one of the last books Joyce read, and it’s is a kind of Doppelgänger to Finnegans Wake.

(2) The book is a record of that generation in Ireland, when the humor could be desperate, when the church was all-powerful, when heavy drinking and homosocial life in crowded dingy pubs had to stand in for the wider international society that Joyce chose.
(3) O’Brien was a member of what the scholar Hugh Kenner called “Irish nihilism.” There is no moral sense in the book, which after all begins with someone’s head being crushed by a garden spade.
(4) O’Brien was a minimalist, and his deepest ties are to Beckett. The Irish journalist Fintan O’Toole argued this in a 2009 review written, for the American public, in The New York Review of Books.

(5) And then there’s O’Brien’s own explanation, that the book is about a dead man and that the last page shows how the damned suffer their punishments eternally. But that’s only an explanation if your idea of hell includes knives so thin they can’t be seen, microscopic carved wooden boxes, and sexually mutable bicycles. Otherwise it doesn’t explain anything.

The fact that people keep coming up with these explanations shows that the book is still too odd to be accepted as a mid-century modernist novel or even an anachronistic postmodern one. It’s quite an accomplishment to remain unclassifiable after almost a hundred years. I’d rather say The Third Policeman is one of the best examples of a genuinely avant-garde modernist work, because—according to the canonical definition of the avant-garde, given by Theodor Adorno—it just won’t fit into categories, even so many years on.

It seems the literary world is full of novels about works of fine art, especially painting: Girl with a Pearl Earring by Tracy Chevalier’s Girl With a Pearl Earring, Donna Tartt’s The Goldfinch, Heather Mariah Webb’s Rodin’s Lover, and in an earlier generation, Irving Stone’s The Agony and the Ecstasy (Michelangelo) and Lust for Life (Van Gogh)—not to mention Proust’s inaccurate memory of Vermeer’s View of Delft.

What these and many others have in common is appreciation for the art. The authors love the artists and the paintings, and their plots revolve around them. Bernhard is a famous contrarian, known for his venomous hatred and impatience of Austria and Austrians. (There’s an entire book, My Prizes, which collects his versions of speeches he made when he accepted literary prizes, skewering and insulting the people and institutions that had given him the awards.)

Reger, the protagonist in Old Masters, visits the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, again and again, just to see one portrait by Tintoretto, but not because he loves it, or it’s sublime, or he’s entranced or mesmerized or overawed… but because the Tintoretto is the only picture in the world that he can stomach. As an art historian, I find that so refreshing. What isn’t tiresome about worship? Why should everyone’s motivation in writing about art be beauty, emotion, or the sublime?

In the book, Reger’s friend goes to meet him, but stops short, seeing him sitting in front of the Tintoretto painting. We read at length about the things Reger dislikes, how he can stomach this one painting, how it’s long been a kind of refuge for him.

Art altogether is nothing but a survival skill… and attempt to cope with this world and its revolting aspects, which, as we know, is only possible by resorting to lies and falsehoods, to hypocrisy and self-deception, Reger said. These pictures are full of lies and falsehoods and full of hypocrisy and self-deception, there is nothing else in them if we disregard their often inspired artistry.
In the end, the two friends agree to go to the theater, and of course they hate what they see.

I hope you might be intrigued by one or another of these. These ten books helped me see just how far novels can stretch, how badly they can misbehave, how much they can torture language, how close they can get to just being irrational. It’s liberating as well as daunting to see a famous author indulge in dialogue as batty as this mock philosophic debate from Ferdydurke:
The anti-Filidor roared: “Noodles, noodles, namely a mixture of flour, eggs, and water!”
Filidor retorted instantly: “Noodle, namely the higher being of the Noodle, the highest Noodle himself!”
His eyes flashed lightning, his beard fluttered, it was clear he had scored a victory.
You can’t eliminate every cliché and commonplace in your writing, but if you have models like these ten books, you’ll stay alert for longer. You might even make it partway across the poppy field.
Stories, Like Illnesses by James Elkins is available from Unnamed Press.
